doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Explaining improvisation as jazz performance practice
summary: He explains that jazz rests on shared conventions of repertory, harmony, voicing, tone, rhythm and licks, and that improvisation is on something such as a harmonic pattern.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Again, very timely that you said that because I just got a gift from a fellow jazz educator of Cannonball Adderley Transcribed Solos. And I was looking, you know, at page after page, there’s not too many rests in there. But I want to pursue the thing about improvising a little bit because there’s a quote from you, “The romantic notion that jazz is generated entirely spontaneously” and it makes me think of people who have asked me and I’ve heard them ask other people, “What is this thing they’re doing? When they play the melody I like it when they play the melody and then they do this stuff. What are they doing?” If you’re at a cocktail party and someone answers that like do you pretend your phone rings and walk away or do you try to answer it?
I pretend my phone rings and I walk away. Sorry. I ducked that question. I could try to not duck the question if you really want me to.

I think — books I haven’t written — I think jazz would do very well to have a book about jazz as performance practice by analogy with Baroque music performance practice. I think there are a huge amount of unspoken agreed conventions in a jazz performance and these are brought to the table when people meet and this is why you have the jazz show go “Let me introduce the band” and then they introduce each other because it’s the first time they’ve played together, and yet they sound great and the person who is not a musician comes up afterwards and says, “You guys sound terrific, how long have you been playing together?” “We just met.” “How did you do that?” You know and the answer to how’d you do that is performance practice. Jazz is as deeply embedded with prior agreements coming to a performance as any music that I know. And that extends to techniques of improvisation. So maybe to talk about what you’re asking me, it’s not just improvisation but it’s repertory, it’s harmony and agreements about what sounds, what voicings are appropriate for jazz and what voicings are inappropriate. It’s instrumentation and tone on instruments. What kind of a sound are you bringing to a jazz gig? It’s rhythmic style, swing, Latin, rock-based, hip hop. There are all sorts of things that people bring into the performance that they have learned to do with others previously, a sort of endless chain, and how you go about improvising for a substantial swath of jazz includes that. There were sort of in the simplest explanation, licks, formulas, things that you use as a way to get started and embellish upon. You don’t just come with a blank slate. I think Mingus made a comment along that line once, though I don’t remember exactly what it was.
I saw it. I think “You have to improvise on something.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Yeah, you’ve got to improvise on something. Yeah. And until free jazz came along and modal jazz with droning harmonies, until those musics came on to open up possibilities for other ways of creating that something that you improvise on, jazz was very much made of improvised melodies that were generated in response to a functional harmonic pattern that underlied, whether that was blues or a popular song, that lay underneath the — that form the structure of the performance on which they’re playing.
